plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: It is specific where a game usually goes wrong and open where a director should decide. It pins down the 10-foot controller-first UI, glyph rules, attract mode, dev mode sliders, code-only audio, the hub protocol and the one-command test rule, but leaves genre and perspective to me. The 'This computer' section was the most useful part: exact tool versions, how to stand in for a controller, a touch device and a second player, and rules for sharing the machine. That let me check the plan's risky assumptions here instead of guessing.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Four things. First, 'Follow the hub docs for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own' can mean either a clean solo fallback or real multiplayer outside the hub, and the protocol page says that outside a session the game is not affected. I planned for both readings. Second, the WebGPU flags in 'This computer' don't work for this engine: with them the page logs 'GPU device lost (Destroyed)' and stays blank while rAF reports 60 fps. The engine's own flags (--use-vulkan=swiftshader --use-angle=swiftshader) work. Third, 'capture its world, characters, themes and tone' sits awkwardly beside 'an original game', so I had to draw my own line: the kinds of mechanics and the tone yes, its names, story, map and content no. Fourth, TASK.md is written to the builder, so a planner has to work out which parts (title process, file names, exit interview) to pass on and which to leave out. STAGE.md settles the title and the names, but not the rest.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: Fitting a game whose identity is a first-person body in a big burning open world onto an engine built around a follow camera and small rooms. It has no first-person camera, no sky, terraced terrain, cars that can't pitch or roll, and a HUD of text lines. I had to decide what to build, in what order, and how to prove the whole thing can be finished, without leaving a builder with questions. The other hard part was writing enough detail to build from without ever being able to see the result: every number and name is a judgement call that nobody can test until a builder has built it. Co-op under the hub's limits (20 messages a second, about 1,200 bytes for an unreliable message) also took real design work.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: Five changes. (1) Correct the WebGPU flags for this engine, or point to the engine's list, since every builder will otherwise lose time on a blank canvas. (2) Say plainly whether multiplayer outside the hub must work across machines, on the same machine, or not at all. (3) Give a rough target for the demo's length and the size of its world, because 'long enough to show ALL features' can justify almost any scope. (4) Say what to cut first when the scope exceeds the budget, since 'no stubs' and 'feature-complete' leave only content counts to trim. (5) Tell the planner directly that building the engine and running short feasibility tests is welcome. 'Whether and how much to research is your choice' covers it, but the most useful findings in my plan came from running things, not reading about them.
